A music student is usually taught that a piece "is in" a scale: C major, A minor, the blues scale. A scale is a list of
notes in order. Hindustani (North Indian) classical music has the word **raga**, and it is often translated "scale", but
that is not what it is. Two ragas can have exactly the same seven notes and be as different as a lullaby and a march. This
lesson shows what a raga carries that a scale does not, and lets you hear the difference.

**How to use the page.** Each widget has buttons that play. The bar at the bottom of the window sets the volume (start low).
Press *Ascent, then descent* to hear the raga; then press *As a plain scale* to hear the same notes with everything
that makes it a raga taken away.

*What has been checked.* The general ideas on this page (a raga is neither a scale nor a tune; ascent and descent; vadi
and samvadi; pakad; ornament; drone; time of day; the ten thaats and 72 melakartas; the 22 shrutis; andolan) were checked on
27 November 2026 against *The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music*, vol. 5 (Ruckert and Widdess, "Hindustani Raga", pp. 64-88;
Kassebaum, "Karnatak Raga"). Garland also confirms the notes of Bhairav, Todi, Bhupali and the Kalyan thaat that Yaman belongs to, and the two Nis
of Khamaj. It does **not** give the ascent and descent of Yaman, Bhupali, Malkauns, Khamaj or Todi, the vadi and samvadi of any
of the six, their times of day (except that Bhairav is a dawn raga), or the ornaments of Bhairav and Todi. Those details are still
*unverified* (from general knowledge; check them with a teacher who plays the raga) and are marked where they come up.
The tuning is this site's model, not Garland's: Garland says the "natural" tuning is similar to Pythagorean, and that
intonation varies with the raga, the singer and the school, so treat the ratios below as a sketch.

## A scale is a list; a raga is a way of moving

Here is what a scale gives you: a set of pitches, an order, and the same order up and down. A raga gives all that, and more:

| | Scale | Raga |
|---|---|---|
| Notes | A set | A set, **but not all used equally** |
| Order | The same up and down | The **ascent (*aroha*)** and **descent (*avaroha*)** can differ: notes skipped going up, or two versions of a note |
| Which notes matter | None in particular (the tonic, perhaps) | The **vadi** ("speaker", the "king": the most prominent note) and **samvadi** ("co-speaker", the "minister": the second, in many ragas a fourth or fifth from it). Garland adds that in practice more than two notes are stressed and the theory is more rigid than the music |
| Phrases | None | **Characteristic phrases** (*pakad*, "catch": a motive that sums up the raga) that identify it, and rules about where to start and rest. To a performer a raga is known mainly by its phrases |
| Ornament | Optional | Part of the note: a slide (***meend***), a slow oscillation (***andolan***), a grace note (***kan***); together, ***gamaka***. Garland confirms slides and andolan; the names *meend* and *kan* are unverified, and *gamaka* is the Karnatak (South Indian) term in Garland |
| Accompaniment | Chords, perhaps | A **drone**, usually Sa and Pa (Ma or Ni instead of Pa in a raga with no Pa), against which every note is heard |
| Time and mood | None | A time of day (or season) and a mood (*rasa*) |
| Tuning | Fixed by the instrument (the piano's) | Heard against the drone; a note can be a little higher or lower in a different raga |

The student writing a scale on paper has no place to write most of these. A raga is passed on by singing it.

## Hearing the notes of a raga

The grid at the top of each widget shows the twelve possible notes: **S r R g G M M♯ P d D n N**. Capital letters are
*shuddha* (natural), lowercase *komal* (flat), and M♯ is *tivra* Ma (sharp). A filled box is used going up and down; a box
with ▲ only going up, ▼ only coming down; a ring marks the vadi, a dashed ring the samvadi.

The first note is **Sa**, which is wherever the performer says it is, as the tonic is on any instrument. Press *Drone* to
hear Sa and Pa sustained underneath; the notes of the raga are heard against it. Choose another Sa with the second menu.

First, **Yaman**. It belongs to the Kalyan thaat, the major scale with a raised fourth (a Lydian scale, to a Western ear). The
page also has it begin its ascent from the low Ni, with Pa passed over going up, and dwell on Ga and Ni (*unverified*):

<div class="sk" data-w="raga" data-title="Raga Yaman" data-set="raga=yaman"></div>

**Bhairav**: komal re and komal dha (Garland lists it as a dawn raga, with this scale up and down). The page gives both komal notes a slow, wide
oscillation (*unverified*: Garland describes andolan only for Darbari Kanada). The notes on the piano are a "double harmonic"
scale; the raga is not that scale. Press *A slide and a wobble* to hear the vadi and samvadi stepped, then joined by a slide, then
swinging:

<div class="sk" data-w="raga" data-title="Raga Bhairav" data-set="raga=bhairav"></div>

**Khamaj** is a clear case where ascent and descent differ: it uses shuddha Ni going up but komal ni coming down (Garland's example of a raised seventh
up and a lowered one down). Leaving out Re going up is *unverified*:

<div class="sk" data-w="raga" data-title="Raga Khamaj" data-set="raga=khamaj"></div>

## The same notes, different ragas

Ragas with five notes show the point most cleanly. **Bhupali** and **Malkauns** each have five notes and each has the
same notes up and down. They are not the same raga as any other five-note scale you know (Bhupali, C D E G A, is the major pentatonic; Garland gives its notes as Sa Re Ga Pa Dha. Malkauns, C E♭ F A♭ B♭, is a different mode of a major pentatonic, the one that starts on its third degree; its notes are unverified), and they sound different from each
other because the music dwells on different notes (the vadi) and approaches them differently (the vadi and samvadi given here are unverified):

<div class="sk" data-w="raga" data-title="Raga Bhupali" data-set="raga=bhupali"></div>

<div class="sk" data-w="raga" data-title="Raga Malkauns" data-set="raga=malkauns"></div>

And **Todi**, with its komal re, ga and dha and tivra Ma (Garland's scale for the Todi thaat and for Miyan ki Todi), is a good example of how far a raga's scale can sit from the major scale:

<div class="sk" data-w="raga" data-title="Raga Todi" data-set="raga=todi"></div>

## Raga and thaat

In the twentieth century V. N. Bhatkhande sorted ragas into ten parent scales, ***thaats***, each a seven-note scale
(Bilawal, Kalyan, Khamaj, Bhairav, Poorvi, Marwa, Kafi, Asavari, Bhairavi and Todi). Yaman belongs to Kalyan, Bhairav
to Bhairav, Khamaj to Khamaj, Todi to Todi. A thaat is a scale, a filing system for ragas, and not a raga: many ragas
share one thaat, and some ragas fit into a thaat only by convention. Garland's example is Bhupali, which could go in Kalyan or Bilaval
(musicians usually relate it to Kalyan); it says the system is derived from the ragas as performed, not the reverse, and that not all
musicians accept it. Where Malkauns is filed is unverified. In Karnatak (South Indian) music the parent scales are
the 72 ***melakartas*** of Venkatamakhi (17th century); players learn ragas from their teachers' compositions, not from the scheme.

## The tuning: pure ratios against a drone

This is the site's model. Garland says only that the "natural" tuning is similar to Pythagorean (not the 5-limit ratios used here) and that
a svara may be pitched a little higher or lower in different ragas. The widgets tune the twelve swaras in simple ratios from Sa: re 16:15, Re 9:8, ga 6:5, Ga 5:4, Ma 4:3, M♯ 45:32,
Pa 3:2, dha 8:5, Dha 5:3, ni 16:9, Ni 15/8. On the piano the thirds, sixths and sevenths are 14 to 16 cents away
from these. Press *Raga in just tuning and on the piano, together*: the slow beating on Ga, Ni and the komal notes is that difference, and
it is a good reason that a fixed-pitch instrument is a poor way to play a raga.

The tradition counts 22 pitches to the octave (*shrutis*), which does not mean twenty-two equal steps: Garland calls them unequal and
says the number, laid down in the earliest treatises, is of doubtful relevance to modern practice; infinite gradations of pitch are used to inflect each of the seven svaras. The exact ratios are argued in the literature
and Garland gives none. The page uses one common reading. See also the lessons on
[tuning systems](tuning-systems.qmd).

## Things to try

1. Play Yaman's *As a plain scale* button. What is missing from it compared to the raga?
2. In Khamaj, find the two Nis in the grid. Which is used going up, which coming down?
3. Change Sa to F♯. The notes change; what stays the same?
4. Press *Both together* in Bhairav. Which notes beat fastest? Which note does not beat at all?
5. Bhupali's vadi is Ga and Malkauns' is Ma (both unverified). Hold each of those notes in turn and play the other four around it: how does the music's centre of gravity change, although both have five notes?
